newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S. wins French pledge on Iraq, but rift remains.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wins French pledge on Iraq, but rift remains.

text.p: The United States on Thursday welcomed a French pledge to rejoin air patrols over Iraq even though the two Gulf War allies remained at odds over U.S. cruise missile strikes on Iraq this week.

"We believe the international coalition is very much in place," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said after Secretary of State Warren Christopher met French President Jacques Chirac and Foreign Minister Herve de Charette in Paris.
"The Secretary is pleased that...France remains part of the coalition," he told reporters.

France, which scaled back its air patrols over Iraq after U.S. missile strikes aimed at punishing President Saddam Hussein for sending troops into Kurdish areas of northern Iraq, said it would resume enforcing the two no-fly zones in Iraq from Monday.
But the French Foreign Ministry snubbed Washington by saying French planes would not help patrol an extended no-fly zone declared by President Bill Clinton in southern Iraq.

French planes would stay south of the 32nd parallel, the former limit of the zone set after the Gulf War. Clinton extended the no-fly zone north to the 33rd parallel, close to Baghdad, a French statement said.
The United States and Britain agreed earlier on Thursday they could patrol the extended no-fly zone over southern Iraq without French help.
"We've got sufficient air assets in the region to implement the extended no-fly zone," Burns said after Christopher met British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind in London.

Britain has strongly supported the United States over Iraq. But France pointedly refused to endorse the raids, causing the most serious rift in the Gulf War coalition that evicted Saddam's troops from Kuwait in 1991.
And the two countries differed over what Christopher said in Paris.

The French Foreign Ministry statement said Christopher "confirmed the end of the American 'Desert Strike' operations in Iraq". And it said the confirmation cleared the way for France to resume its air patrols.
A senior State Department official told reporters after double-checking with Christopher: "The Secretary of State did not say in the meetings today that 'Desert Strike' is over."
Asked to explain the apparent discrepancy, the official said it might be "linguistic".
And spokesman Burns said that: "American policy and American actions will be based very much on what Saddam Hussein does...We retain the option and the right to use force if necessary."

Christopher and de Charette earlier declined to talk about Iraq at a news conference, preferring to stress unity on a wide range of international issues including Bosnia, NATO reform and efforts to outlaw nuclear testing.

France played a key part in enforcing the initial no-fly zone. But it said on Wednesday its planes were staying south of the 30th parallel while it studied the implications of the unilateral American decision to extend the zone.
And officials said French planes suspended reconnaissance flights in the separate zone over northern Iraq, including the Kurdish battle zone, on Tuesday when the U.S. first struck.

Britain's Rifkind took a veiled swipe at the French in a BBC radio interview, saying: "Criticism of the Americans is easy, but coming from people who have not an alternative strategy it is far from convincing."
Christopher said the 33 cruise missiles fired at Iraq on Tuesday and Wednesday had been an effective response to Baghdad.
After his talks in Paris, Christopher flew to Germany, where he will meet Chancellor Helmut Kohl and deliver a lecture on European security.
